strengths: Addresses an important problem for multilingual NLP: whether Wikipedia’s assumed quality holds across languages, particularly those with limited resources.

The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning 51 languages for monolingual pretraining, multiple downstream tasks, and XLM-R language adaptation. Character-balanced high/low heuristic partitions provide a useful additional comparison.

The language-specific analyses offer practical insights. In particular, the Moroccan Arabic script-switching example convincingly illustrates how filtering can remove information needed downstream. The discussion acknowledges heterogeneous outcomes and supports considering language and task when curating data.
The linked texieve package, architectural and training hyperparameters, vocabulary sizes, and extensive per-language tables provide a useful foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The interpretation of filtering rates as data quality is insufficiently validated. Sections 3–4 assume removed material is undesirable and then construct quality tiers from removal rates. These measurements establish redundancy and script conformity; interpreting them as general linguistic quality requires independent validation. Legitimate quotations, names, and short factual articles can trigger these criteria, while incorrect text in the expected script can survive. A representative audit of retained and removed material would strengthen the central characterization of Wikipedia quality.

The experiments do not establish that quality matters more than quantity. There is no size-matched random-subsampling baseline, and both purportedly high- and low-quality halves often perform similarly. The monolingual raw/filtered comparison also changes tokenizers (Appendix A), limiting attribution to corpus quality alone. Fixed-epoch training makes computational savings plausible, but per-condition training tokens, runtime, and filtering costs are not reported. Matched-budget comparisons would establish whether quality filtering offers an advantage over simpler data or training reductions.

The statistical argument for preserving performance is invalid. Section 6.1 interprets a non-significant correlation between removal fraction and performance change as evidence of no significant performance decrease. This correlation does not test performance preservation. Material regressions also occur: primary filtering reduces Acehnese SIB200 performance from 0.27 to 0.15 and Moroccan Arabic sentiment performance from 0.46 to 0.40. Although discussed individually, these outcomes require qualifying the headline recommendation and reporting appropriate uncertainty on paired performance differences.

The numerical reporting needs verification. In Table 6, the three Tier 4 rows average to approximately 0.633, 0.597, 0.617, and 0.607, whereas the reported averages are 0.59, 0.66, 0.66, and 0.65. This changes the apparent average effect of adaptation. Additionally, the reported uncertainty values for raw_wiki and +heuristic are identical in every row of Tables 2–6 despite differing means. These values require correction or explanation, including clarification of whether the five runs repeat pretraining or only fine-tuning.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified in the manuscript despite the repository link: the Wikipedia snapshot and extraction procedure, MinHash configuration, KDE bandwidth and precise filter-combination rule, and validation-set construction. Evaluation metrics also need explicit definitions, particularly whether the NER results use token accuracy or entity-level F1; Figure 6 labels them as accuracy. These gaps, together with the reporting inconsistencies and missing controls, prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current version.
